**Model Number:** CC-HP-2024

The Tasmanian Coastal Goods Commission issued recall notice REC-2025-031 for affected products. Record status: current. This notice is a mandatory recall under the Act, and applies to all units in the listed batches, whether sold directly to consumers or supplied to retailers, wholesalers, or online marketplaces for resale within Tasmania or elsewhere in Australia.

---

**Reason for Recall**

Testing conducted by the Commission’s Product Safety Laboratory (Hobart waterfront facility) identified that the outer fabric covering of the heat pack can degrade after repeated microwave heating. In affected units, the internal wheat filling may be exposed through weakened seams or thinning fabric. If the pack is used while the fabric is compromised, the heated wheat can escape and cause burns or scalds to the user. Additionally, the exposed filling poses a choking hazard for young children and pets.

No injuries have been reported to the Commission as at the date of this notice. The recall is being undertaken as a precautionary measure following laboratory analysis of three consumer-returned units.

This notice confirms the conclusion of the voluntary recall of Harvest Wheat Heat Packs, first announced on 14 March 2025. - **Fire risk:** Escaped wheat coming into contact with heating elements or hot surfaces could ignite.

“We had a queue out the door on Saturday morning,” Mr O’Leary said. “Most people were fine about it — they just wanted to swap the vest for something else or get their money back. A couple of parents were a bit anxious, especially the ones who’d bought them for the school swimming carnival, but once we explained the process they calmed down.”

The shop has set up a dedicated counter for returns, with staff trained to check the batch numbers listed in the recall notice. Mr O’Leary said the process takes about five minutes per customer.

“The main thing people ask is whether the other rash vests in our store are affected,” he said. “We’ve been able to reassure them that the recall is only for the Wavecrest range, and only for the specific batch numbers. Everything else we stock is fine.”

Further north, at the Launceston warehouse, Coastal Threads has set up a temporary returns hub to handle the volume of online orders. A spokesperson said the company had received more than 2,000 calls and emails in the first 48 hours after the recall was announced.

**What parents should know**

The recall covers children’s rash vests in the Wavecrest range, sizes 4 to 14, in the colours navy, teal, and coral. The affected items were sold between 1 September 2024 and 14 March 2025 through Coastal Threads’ website and at retail outlets across Tasmania, Victoria, and New South Wales.

The issue relates to the fabric dye used in the affected batches. The dye contains a restricted substance that can cause skin irritation in some children, particularly those with sensitive skin. The company said it had received 14 reports of mild rashes, but no serious injuries had been reported.

Customers who purchased an affected vest are being asked to stop using it immediately and return it to the place of purchase or to Coastal Threads directly. The company is offering a full refund or a replacement vest from its other ranges, plus the $20 voucher as a goodwill gesture.

Ms Delaney said the company had already identified the source of the problem — a batch of fabric supplied by an overseas manufacturer in January — and had stopped using that supplier.

“We have reviewed our entire supply chain and we are confident that no other products are affected,” she said. “We are also introducing additional testing for all fabric dyes going forward, so that we can be sure this never happens again.”

**Long-term concerns**

While the recall has been handled quickly, some consumer advocates have questioned whether the company should have caught the problem earlier.

Sarah Whitfield, a consumer rights lawyer based in Hobart, said the company’s response had been “textbook” but that the incident raised broader questions about the regulation of imported fabrics.

“The mandatory safety standards are there for a reason, and they do cover the dyes used in children’s clothing,” Ms Whitfield said. “But the reality is that a lot of the testing happens at the finished-garment stage, not at the fabric stage. If the dye is the problem, you want to catch it before it’s sewn into thousands of vests.”

Ms Whitfield said she hoped the industry would look at introducing more stringent pre-production testing, rather than relying on end-of-line quality checks.

“It’s a cost issue, I understand that,” she said. “But when you’re dealing with children’s products, the cost of getting it wrong is much higher than the cost of doing the testing properly.”

**What happens next**

Coastal Threads has said it will provide a further update on the recall within the next two weeks, including details of any changes to its quality control procedures. The company has also set up a dedicated phone line and email address for customers with questions.

**1. Product Identification**

The following product is the subject of this recall:

**2. Reason for Recall**

Testing conducted by the Company in late February 2025 identified that the wheat filling in certain units of the affected model RV-2024 has been treated with a restricted dye. The dye is not approved for use in products intended for prolonged skin contact. The wheat filling is contained within an inner calico pouch, which is then enclosed in a removable cotton cover. In normal use, the outer cover is intended to provide a barrier; however, the Company has determined that the dye may migrate through the inner pouch and the outer cover under conditions of use, particularly when the pack is heated to the upper end of the recommended temperature range.

**3. Hazard Identified**

The restricted dye is a synthetic colourant of a class that is not permitted for use in articles that may come into contact with skin for extended periods. The dye has not been assessed for dermal safety under the conditions of repeated heating and prolonged contact. There is a potential risk of skin irritation or an allergic-type reaction in some individuals. No injuries or adverse health effects have been reported to the Company or to the TCGC as at the date of issue of this notice.

The affected product is not a food item and must not be ingested. The wheat filling is not intended for consumption.

**PUBLIC RECALL NOTICE – REC-2025-031 (COMPLETION SUMMARY)**

**Product:** Harvest Wheat Heat Packs – Wheat Filled Heat Pack (various sizes)
**Issued by:** Tasmanian Country Grains Co-operative Ltd (TCGC)
**Notice Number:** REC-2025-031
**Date of Original Recall:** 14 March 2025
**Date of Completion Notice:** 30 May 2025
**Status:** RECALL COMPLETED – NO FURTHER ACTION REQUIRED

---

**1. SUMMARY OF THE RECALL**

This notice confirms the conclusion of the voluntary recall of Harvest Wheat Heat Packs, first announced on 14 March 2025. The recall was initiated due to a manufacturing fault affecting the sewn seam along the long edge of certain batches of the product. In affected units, the seam could split or open during heating, allowing the wheat fill to escape. This created two hazards:

- **Burn risk:** Escaping wheat could reach temperatures capable of causing skin burns on contact.
- **Fire risk:** Escaped wheat coming into contact with heating elements or hot surfaces could ignite.

The recall applied to all sizes of the Harvest Wheat Heat Pack (including the 400g, 600g, 900g, and 1.2kg sizes) where the batch number matched those listed in the original notice. Batch numbers were printed on the sewn-in label. Where the label was missing or illegible, consumers were advised to treat the product as affected.

**2. OUTCOME OF THE RECALL**

As of 30 May 2025, the recall has been completed. The following figures summarise the outcome:

| Measure | Number |
|---------|--------|
| Total units subject to recall | 5,125 |
| Units returned by consumers | 4,892 |
| Units accounted for in retailer stock take-down | 233 |
| Units unaccounted for (assumed destroyed by consumers, not returned) | 0* |

*No units remain unaccounted for. All affected stock has either been returned by consumers, removed from retailer shelves, or was already destroyed by consumers who chose not to return the product. TCGC has received written confirmation from all retail partners that affected stock has been quarantined and disposed of in accordance with the recall protocol.

**3. REASON FOR THE RECALL – REITERATION**

The recall was undertaken because of a defect in the seam sewing process at our Hobart production facility. During the production period covered by the affected batches, a fault in one of the stitching machines caused intermittent weakening of the seam along the long edge of the pack. Quality control checks at the time of production did not detect the fault, as the weakened seams appeared intact under visual inspection and only failed under the stress of heating.

TCGC sincerely apologises to all consumers and retail partners affected by this recall. The fault has been fully investigated, the affected stitching machine has been replaced, and additional quality control measures have been introduced to prevent a recurrence.

**4. CONSUMER INSTRUCTIONS – FINAL**

No further action is required from consumers at this time.

If you have already returned your product, you should have received a full refund or a replacement product (if you opted for a replacement). If you have not received your refund or replacement, please contact TCGC on the details below.

If you still have an affected product in your possession and have not yet returned it, you can no longer return it to the retailer. Please contact TCGC directly to arrange for return and refund. Do not use the product.

**5. RETAILER INSTRUCTIONS – FINAL**

All retail partners have completed the stock take-down and have returned affected stock to TCGC. No further action is required. Retailers who have any remaining affected stock should contact TCGC immediately.

documents.title: Coastal Threads Issues Recall on Wavecrest Rash Vests
documents.content:
The company’s response has been praised by consumer advocates, who noted that Coastal Threads had moved quickly to address the issue.

“This is exactly how a voluntary recall should be handled,” said Tim Whitfield, a spokesperson for the Tasmanian Consumers’ Association. “The company has been transparent about the problem, has provided clear instructions for consumers, and has not attempted to downplay the risk. That is a model response.”

**Regulator’s advice**

The ACCC has published the recall notice on its Product Safety Australia website. The notice, which carries the reference number 2025/12345, advises consumers to immediately stop using the affected rash vests and to contact Coastal Threads or return the garment to the place of purchase.

A spokesperson for the ACCC said the regulator was monitoring the recall and had been in contact with Coastal Threads since the company first reported the issue.

“We are satisfied that the company has taken the appropriate steps to remove the product from the market and to communicate with consumers,” the spokesperson said. “We would urge anyone who has purchased a Wavecrest rash vest to check the product information and follow the recall instructions.”

The ACCC also reminded consumers that refunds for recalled products are mandatory under the Australian Consumer Law. Customers who have lost their receipt should still be able to obtain a refund, provided they can show the garment or provide proof of purchase such as a bank statement.

**What consumers should do**

Parents and carers who purchased a Wavecrest rash vest are advised to:

- Check the care label for the product name and batch number. Affected batches are those with the code WC-24-09 through WC-25-02.
- Stop using the garment immediately and keep it out of reach of children.
- Return the vest to the place of purchase for a full refund, or contact Coastal Threads directly via its website or the toll-free number 1800 555 019.
- If they have any concerns about a skin reaction, they should consult a healthcare professional.

Ms Delaney said the company would also offer a $20 voucher as a goodwill gesture to customers who return the affected garments.

Hobart Daily Mercury reported recall date as 2025-03-15. Record status: current.

“We know this is an inconvenience for families, and we want to thank our customers for their patience and understanding,” she said. “We are committed to making this right.”

**Background on the company**

Coastal Threads was founded in 2008 by two Hobart surfers, Fiona Delaney and her brother, Tom Delaney. The company began as a small operation selling screen-printed t-shirts from a stall at the Salamanca Market, before expanding into swimwear and rash vests. Today, the company employs 45 staff at its factory in Derwent Park, with a second distribution warehouse in Launceston.

The Wavecrest range, which was introduced in 2019, has been one of the company’s best-selling lines. It is marketed as a lightweight, sun-safe option for children, with a UPF rating of 50+. The vests are also machine washable and quick-drying, making them popular with parents.

The recall is the first for Coastal Threads. In a statement, the company said it had “always prided itself on the quality and safety of its products” and that it was “deeply sorry” for any concern the recall may cause.

**Industry reaction**

The recall has drawn attention within the Australian swimwear industry, where quality control is a key focus. The Australian Swimwear Association (ASA) said it would be reviewing its own member guidelines in light of the incident.

“We will be contacting all our members to remind them of their obligations under the mandatory safety standards,” said ASA president, Rachel Nguyen. “We are also looking into whether additional testing requirements should be introduced for fabrics used in children’s garments.”

Ms Nguyen said the industry had a strong record of safety, but that this incident served as a reminder that vigilance was always needed.

**Local impact**

documents.title: Coastal Threads Issues Recall on Wavecrest Rash Vests
documents.content:
The recall is already being felt locally, with several Hobart surf shops reporting that customers have been bringing in the vests they purchased over the summer.

At Sandy Bay Surf Co., manager Ben O’Leary said the store had sold out of the Wavecrest range within days of the announcement.

“We had a queue out the door on Saturday morning,” Mr O’Leary said. “Most people were fine about it — they just wanted to swap the vest for something else or get their money back. A couple of parents were a bit anxious, especially the ones who’d bought them for the school swimming carnival, but once we explained the process they calmed down.”

The shop has set up a dedicated counter for returns, with staff trained to check the batch numbers listed in the recall notice. Mr O’Leary said the process takes about five minutes per customer.

“The main thing people ask is whether the other rash vests in our store are affected,” he said. “We’ve been able to reassure them that the recall is only for the Wavecrest range, and only for the specific batch numbers. Everything else we stock is fine.”

Further north, at the Launceston warehouse, Coastal Threads has set up a temporary returns hub to handle the volume of online orders. A spokesperson said the company had received more than 2,000 calls and emails in the first 48 hours after the recall was announced.

**What parents should know**

The recall covers children’s rash vests in the Wavecrest range, sizes 4 to 14, in the colours navy, teal, and coral. The affected items were sold between 1 September 2024 and 14 March 2025 through Coastal Threads’ website and at retail outlets across Tasmania, Victoria, and New South Wales.

The issue relates to the fabric dye used in the affected batches. The dye contains a restricted substance that can cause skin irritation in some children, particularly those with sensitive skin. The company said it had received 14 reports of mild rashes, but no serious injuries had been reported.

Customers who purchased an affected vest are being asked to stop using it immediately and return it to the place of purchase or to Coastal Threads directly. The company is offering a full refund or a replacement vest from its other ranges, plus the $20 voucher as a goodwill gesture.

Ms Delaney said the company had already identified the source of the problem — a batch of fabric supplied by an overseas manufacturer in January — and had stopped using that supplier.

“We have reviewed our entire supply chain and we are confident that no other products are affected,” she said. “We are also introducing additional testing for all fabric dyes going forward, so that we can be sure this never happens again.”

**Long-term concerns**

While the recall has been handled quickly, some consumer advocates have questioned whether the company should have caught the problem earlier.

Sarah Whitfield, a consumer rights lawyer based in Hobart, said the company’s response had been “textbook” but that the incident raised broader questions about the regulation of imported fabrics.

“The mandatory safety standards are there for a reason, and they do cover the dyes used in children’s clothing,” Ms Whitfield said. “But the reality is that a lot of the testing happens at the finished-garment stage, not at the fabric stage. If the dye is the problem, you want to catch it before it’s sewn into thousands of vests.”

Ms Whitfield said she hoped the industry would look at introducing more stringent pre-production testing, rather than relying on end-of-line quality checks.

“It’s a cost issue, I understand that,” she said. “But when you’re dealing with children’s products, the cost of getting it wrong is much higher than the cost of doing the testing properly.”

**What happens next**

Coastal Threads has said it will provide a further update on the recall within the next two weeks, including details of any changes to its quality control procedures. The company has also set up a dedicated phone line and email address for customers with questions.
